subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Misinformation Effect
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Misinformation Effect.

hook.text: Witnesses saw a car pass a yield sign. Asked about the stop sign, many remembered a stop sign. It wasn't there.

buildup.text: Elizabeth Loftus showed that misleading questions after an event alter what people believe they saw.

discovery.text: Post-event information gets woven into the original memory. People can't tell real from implanted details.

twist.text: Confidence has no link to accuracy. Witnesses who are most certain are often most wrong.

climax.text: This has freed hundreds of wrongly convicted prisoners whose convictions rested on eyewitness testimony.

punchline.text: What you remember may not be what happened.

details.summary: Post-event information can alter memories of the original event. Elizabeth Loftus demonstrated that leading questions and misleading details introduced after an event become incorporated into eyewitness memory, sometimes permanently.
details.whyItMatters: The misinformation effect has wrongly convicted innocent people. It reveals that memory is reconstructive, not like a video recording, and is vulnerable to contamination at every stage.
takeaways: Post-event information alters memories of the original event
Elizabeth Loftus demonstrated the effect with eyewitness studies
People genuinely believe the distorted memory is accurate

faq.question: How did Loftus demonstrate the misinformation effect?
faq.answer: Participants watched a car accident video, then received questionnaires with misleading information, like asking how fast the cars were going when they smashed versus hit. The smashed group reported higher speeds and were more likely to falsely remember broken glass.

faq.question: Can misinformation create entirely false memories?
faq.answer: Yes. Loftus's lost in the mall study implanted a completely false childhood memory of being lost in a shopping center. About 25 percent of participants developed detailed false memories of the event. Repeated suggestion and imagination can create vivid, confident false memories.
